title: Coding Basics · Episode 2
chapters: Turing and the problems no computer can solve
Why there are so many programming languages
Open source: the free code running the world

units.t: Coding Basics. Episode two.
In this episode: Algorithms, explained, Turing and the problems no computer can solve, Why there are so many programming languages and Open source: the free code running the world.
Part one. Algorithms, explained.
The word sounds futuristic, but it comes from a scholar in 9th-century Baghdad, and you use algorithms every time you look up a word or take the fastest route home.
What an algorithm is.
An algorithm is a precise method for getting something done.
School long division is one: follow the steps and you get the answer every time.
So is the way you find a name in a phone book.
Code is how an algorithm is written for a computer, but the algorithm is the idea behind it.
A good one must be unambiguous, must finish, and must produce the right result.
The word comes from al-Khwarizmi, a Persian mathematician working in Baghdad in the 9th century, whose books on calculation spread through Europe in Latin.
Around 300 BC, Euclid described a method for finding the largest number dividing two others.
It is still taught and used inside some encryption that protects online banking.
Searching and sorting.
Guess a number from 1 to 100, told 'higher' or 'lower' each time.
Guessing 1, 2, 3 could take 100 tries.
Guessing 50, then 25 or 75, halves the possibilities each time.
This is binary search, and it always finds the number within seven guesses.
Among a million sorted items, it needs only about 20 steps.
It only works if items are in order, so computers spend much effort sorting.
Bubble sort swaps neighbouring items that are out of order, repeating until none remain.
It works but is painfully slow on big lists.
Merge sort splits the list in half, sorts each half, then merges them, like combining two sorted piles of exam papers.
On a million items, it can be tens of thousands of times faster.
Why efficiency matters.
Computer scientists care less about speed on ten items than about how the work grows as the data grows.
Some algorithms double their work when the data doubles.
Others quadruple it, and some grow so explosively that even the fastest supercomputer could not finish before the sun burns out.
This is why choosing the right algorithm often matters more than buying a faster computer.
A clever method on an old laptop can beat a clumsy method in a data centre.
Programmers describe this growth with a notation called 'Big O'.
Maps and feeds.
When a map app plots the fastest drive from Parramatta to Bondi, it solves a shortest-path problem.
Roads become a network of points and connections, each with a travel time.
In 1956 the Dutch computer scientist Edsger Dijkstra devised a method for this, reportedly in about 20 minutes at a cafe in Amsterdam.
Modern apps use faster descendants, plus live traffic from other phones, to reroute you around a crash.
By 'the algorithm', people usually mean ranking systems on social media, video and shopping sites.
They use signals such as what you watched, liked, shared or lingered on to predict what you'll engage with.
Early Google search used PageRank, which treated links as votes of importance.
Because feeds optimise for engagement, they can favour content that provokes strong emotions, which is a real and debated concern.
Algorithms in your life.
Knowing how algorithms work gives you some control.
Feed algorithms learn from your behaviour, so deliberately following, muting and choosing 'not interested' changes what you see.
Pausing on outrage teaches the system to show more of it.
Algorithmic thinking also helps offline.
Looking for a lost item?
Search systematically, room by room, rather than randomly.
Packing a car boot?
Big items first is a simple algorithm that usually works well.
Breaking a messy task into clear, repeatable steps is exactly what programmers do, and it works just as well in a kitchen or an office.
The key idea: An algorithm is a clear, step-by-step method for solving a problem, and the idea exists apart from any code.
Part two. Turing and the problems no computer can solve.
Before electronic computers existed, a 23-year-old mathematician proved there are questions no computer, however powerful, will ever be able to answer.
Hilbert's challenge.
In 1928 David Hilbert and Wilhelm Ackermann posed the Entscheidungsproblem, or ‘decision problem’.
Could a definite step-by-step procedure decide whether any statement in formal logic is provable?
If so, mathematics could in principle be mechanised.
In 1931 Kurt Gödel had shown that any consistent system rich enough for arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove, but the decision problem was a separate question.
Answering it needed a precise definition of ‘mechanical procedure’.
In 1936 Alan Turing, a 23-year-old fellow of King's College, Cambridge, supplied one.
He imagined a simple machine: an endless tape of squares, a head that reads, writes or erases one symbol at a time and moves left or right, and a finite table of rules.
Anything that can be calculated by a precise procedure, he argued, such a machine can calculate.
One machine for all.
Turing's paper, ‘On Computable Numbers’, held a second startling idea.
The rule table of any Turing machine can itself be written down as symbols on a tape.
So a universal machine, given a description of any other machine plus its input, can simulate it step by step and produce the same result.
One machine can do the work of every machine, if it is handed the right instructions.
That is exactly what a modern computer is.
Your laptop needs no different hardware to be a word processor, a game or a calculator; it simply loads a different program.
Historians debate how directly Turing's abstract idea influenced the engineers who built the first stored-program computers in the late 1940s, but the concept existed in 1936.
The program that never stops.
Anyone who has watched a frozen app knows that programs can get stuck in endless loops.
A perfect checker, able to examine any program and its input and say in advance whether it will stop or run forever, would be enormously useful.
Some cases are easy: a program that counts from one to ten halts, while ‘repeat forever’ does not.
Others are fiendish.
Imagine a program that searches for an even number greater than 2 that is not the sum of two primes, and stops only if it finds one.
Whether it ever halts depends on Goldbach's conjecture, unsolved since 1742.
A perfect halting checker would settle such questions instantly.
This is the halting problem.
A proof by contradiction.
Suppose someone claims to have built a perfect checker, called H. In the form usually taught today, the argument runs like this.
Build a program called Contrary that takes any program, asks H whether it halts when given its own code, and then does the opposite.
If H says it halts, Contrary loops forever; if H says it loops, Contrary stops.
Now feed Contrary its own code.
Whatever H predicts, Contrary does the reverse, so H is wrong.
No such H can exist.
Turing used reasoning of this kind to answer Hilbert: no general mechanical procedure can decide every mathematical question.
The American logician Alonzo Church reached the same conclusion independently, by a different route, shortly before.
Living with the impossible.
The halting problem is no quirk of old mathematics.

A later result, Rice's theorem, extends it: no program can perfectly decide, for every possible program, any meaningful property of how that program behaves, such as whether it will ever leak a password.
That is why no antivirus software can be guaranteed to catch every piece of malicious code, and why tools that check programs for bugs must accept limits.
They can miss problems, raise false alarms or give up on some cases.
In practice, engineers work around this with time limits, careful restrictions and checkers that are right most of the time.
Turing's 1936 insight remains a humbling boundary.
Some questions are not merely hard for computers.
They are impossible.
The key idea: Turing answered Hilbert's decision problem by first defining exactly what a mechanical procedure is.
Part three. Why there are so many programming languages.
There are thousands of programming languages, from Python to COBOL.
Here's why, and which ones actually run your world.
Bridging people and machines.
A processor only understands machine code: long strings of ones and zeros representing basic operations such as adding two numbers.
Writing that by hand is slow and error-prone.
Programming languages sit in the middle.
They let people write with words and symbols closer to human thinking, then translate them into machine code.
The earliest programmers in the 1940s worked almost directly with machine instructions.
FORTRAN, released by IBM in 1957 and led by John Backus, was one of the first widely used high-level languages, built for heavy maths.
COBOL followed in 1959 for business record-keeping, influenced by Grace Hopper.
It still runs many banks, insurers and agencies, because rewriting decades of reliable code is risky and expensive.
Why so many.
Thousands of languages have been created, though only a few dozen are in wide everyday use.
Why not one for everything?
For the same reason there isn't one tool in a shed.
A hammer and a screwdriver both help you build, but suit different jobs.
Some languages are designed for raw speed, giving close control over memory and hardware.
Others prioritise safety, catching mistakes before the program runs.
Some are easy to read and quick to write.
Others specialise in one domain, such as databases or statistics.
Every design choice is a trade-off, and new languages appear when people want a different balance.
Compiled or interpreted.
There are two broad ways to turn code into something a computer can run.
A compiled language, such as C, C++, Rust or Go, is translated in full before it runs, like translating a whole book before publishing.
The result usually runs very fast.
An interpreted language, like Python, is translated while the program runs, more like a live interpreter at a meeting.
That makes experimenting easier, but it often runs more slowly.
In practice the line has blurred, and many modern languages, including JavaScript in web browsers, use clever mixtures of both.
Well-known languages.
Python, created by Guido van Rossum and released in 1991, is named after Monty Python, not the snake.
It has readable code and is widely used in data analysis, science, automation and AI.
JavaScript was created by Brendan Eich at Netscape in 1995, famously in about ten days.
Despite the name, it has little to do with Java; the name was largely marketing.
It runs in every major browser.
Swift, from Apple in 2014, builds iPhone and Mac apps.
Kotlin is Google's preferred language for Android, alongside the older Java, also common in large business systems.
SQL asks questions of databases, such as 'show all customers in Victoria'.
C, created in the early 1970s at Bell Labs, remains the foundation of operating systems like Linux.
C# suits business software and Unity games.
Learning your first.
Languages are more alike than they look.
Nearly all have variables, conditions, loops and functions.
Once you understand these in one, a second is mostly new spelling and grammar, like learning Spanish after Italian.
Employers generally care more about problem-solving than any single language.
The hard part isn't memorising commands but breaking problems into small, precise steps.
If you want to try coding, pick one language and stick with it.
Python is a common first choice because it reads almost like English.
For websites, start with HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
Free courses are plentiful, and Australian public libraries often run coding sessions.
Build small things you care about, like a budget calculator.
Expect to feel stuck often; that is simply what programming feels like.
The key idea: Programming languages let people write instructions in readable form that are translated into the machine code a processor runs.
Part four. Open source: the free code running the world.
Much of the digital world runs on software written in the open and given away.
In 2024, one engineer's curiosity about a half-second delay showed both the strength and the fragility of that system.
Recipes anyone can read.
Software begins as source code, instructions written in a programming language.
Most commercial programs are distributed only in compiled form, which computers can run but humans can barely read, so the recipe stays secret.
Open source software publishes the recipe.
Anyone can study it, fix it, improve it or build on it, under a licence that sets the rules.
Some licences let you do almost anything; others require you to share your changes too.
Open source does not mean nobody is paid.
Many developers are employed by companies that rely on the software.
But the code itself is shared, and it is everywhere: phones, cars, televisions, routers and the servers behind most websites.
From printer to Linux.
By the late 1970s software was increasingly locked up as a commercial product.
Richard Stallman, an MIT programmer, later described a formative frustration: a jamming laser printer he could not fix because the maker would not share the source code.
In 1983 he announced the GNU project to build a complete operating system of free software, and in 1985 founded the Free Software Foundation.
'Free' meant freedom, not price.
His GNU General Public License required shared changes to stay free, a twist nicknamed copyleft.
GNU still lacked a kernel.
In August 1991 Linus Torvalds, a 21-year-old Helsinki student, posted that he was writing a free operating system, just a hobby, not big and professional like GNU.
Programmers worldwide sent improvements, and Linux was born.
He later created Git too.
Running the world.
Linux is far more widespread than most people realise.
Android, the world's most popular phone system, is built on the Linux kernel.
Linux runs most of the servers behind websites and cloud services, and since 2017 every one of the 500 fastest supercomputers on the TOP500 list has run it.
Open source also supplies browser engines, databases, programming languages and the encryption libraries protecting online banking.
Companies build on this shared foundation rather than writing everything from scratch.
Even firms that once feared open source came around.
Microsoft's chief executive Steve Ballmer called Linux 'a cancer' in 2001; Microsoft later became one of open source's biggest contributors.
Holding up the internet.
Shared code has a weakness: everyone uses it, but no one in particular is responsible for it.
In 2014 researchers discovered Heartbleed, a serious flaw in OpenSSL, encryption software used by a large share of secure web servers.
The project was run by a handful of people, with only one working on it full time, and received only around 2000 US dollars a year in donations.
In 2021 another severe flaw, Log4Shell, turned up in Log4j, a widely used logging tool maintained largely by volunteers.
Each crisis pushed companies and governments to fund critical projects more seriously.
A popular web cartoon sums up the worry: digital infrastructure balanced on one small project that a lone volunteer has thanklessly maintained for years.
Half a second.

In March 2024 Andres Freund, a Microsoft engineer who works on the PostgreSQL database, noticed something odd: logging in to a test machine used more processor time than it should, adding about half a second.
Curious, he traced the delay to xz Utils, a small compression tool in many Linux systems.
Someone had hidden a backdoor in it that could have let an attacker take control of affected servers.
The culprit, using the name Jia Tan, had spent around two years earning the trust of the project's overstretched volunteer maintainer before gaining the access to slip it in.
It was caught before reaching the stable versions of major Linux distributions.
Who was behind it remains unknown, though many security experts suspect a well-resourced, possibly state-backed group.
The key idea: Open source software publishes its source code so anyone can study, change and share it under a licence.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What three things must a good algorithm do?
Answer. Be unambiguous, finish, and give the right result.
Question two. Why did Turing need to describe his imaginary machine to answer Hilbert?
Answer. A 'mechanical procedure' had to be defined first.
Question three. Why do programming languages exist?
Answer. They let people write readable code that gets translated.
Question four. What makes software open source?
Answer. Its source code is public to study and change.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
